title: Section 1.5: Advanced Rational Addition & Subtraction (Part 2)
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 10 • Section 1.5 (Workbook p. 17)

instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### Advanced Rational Denominators (Workbook p. 17)
When denominators contain higher variable powers or multiple terms:
1. **Take the highest power of each variable factor** (e.g. $x$ and $x^4 \implies \text{LCD has } x^4$).
2. **Binomial Numerator Trap:** When subtracting fractions with binomial numerators:
$$\frac{A}{C} - \frac{B + D}{C} = \frac{A - (B + D)}{C} = \frac{A - B - D}{C}$$
**The negative sign MUST distribute to every term in the numerator!**
pitfall: **Fatal Trap:** Writing $\frac{5 - x - 3}{x}$. You must distribute the subtraction to get $+3$!
script:
[Prof. Park] Welcome everyone to Lecture 10 of M090 Introductory Algebra! I am Professor Eunju Park, and joining me at the teaching desk is TA Sora. Today, we take our rational expression skills to the master level in Section 1.5 Part 2, found on workbook page 17: Advanced Rational Addition and Subtraction.

[TA Sora] Hello everyone! Today's lecture addresses the problems that students find most challenging in Unit 1: expressions with higher-degree variable denominators like x^4, three fractions added together simultaneously, and fractions with entire binomials in their numerators.

[Prof. Park] When an entire binomial is in a numerator, subtracting fractions requires distributing a negative sign across multiple terms. If you master today's six examples, you will be completely prepared for every rational expression on your exams. That is right, Sora.

[TA Sora] In engineering and physical science, compound rate equationsâlike calculating the equivalent electrical resistance of multiple parallel circuits, 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3, or computing shared work rates when multiple construction crews pave Montana highwaysârely directly on combining three or more rational terms.

[Prof. Park] For instance, if Crew A takes x hours to pave a section of Highway 191 near Big Sky, and Crew B takes 2x hours, their combined hourly paving rate is 1/x + 1/(2x) = 3/(2x)! Let's look at slide 2 to begin with Example 3A!

[TA Sora] Culvert hydraulics under mountain passes like Bozeman Pass or Reynolds Pass along the Madison River deal with turbulent water flow during spring snowmelt. If an engineer models outflow rates with composite rational expressions, every single minus sign represents back-pressure or friction loss.

[Prof. Park] Misplacing a single minus sign turns a subtraction into an addition, predicting double drainage when in fact water is backing up! That is why civil engineers and algebra students alike treat binomial numerators with absolute structural respect.

[TA Sora] Take your time with every step here. Writing out intermediate lines is the secret to 100% accuracy!

[TA Sora] Exactly! Protect your signs, trust the algebra rules, and you will get the correct answer every single time!

title: Example 3A: Quadratic Monomial Denominator
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 10 • Section 1.5 Example 3A (Workbook p. 17)
detail: Lecture 10: Rational Expressions (Higher Powers & Binomial Numerators)
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### Add or subtract the expression and simplify (Workbook p. 17)
$$\frac{3}{7x^2} + \frac{5}{14x}$$
solution:
$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Step 1: } & \text{Find LCD:} \\
& \text{Coefficients: } \text{LCM}(7, 14) = 14 \\
& \text{Variables: Highest power between } x^2 \text{ and } x \text{ is } x^2 \implies \mathbf{\text{LCD} = 14x^2} \\[0.8em]
\text{Step 2: } & \text{Build common denominator:} \\
& \frac{3 \cdot 2}{7x^2 \cdot 2} + \frac{5 \cdot x}{14x \cdot x} = \frac{6}{14x^2} + \frac{5x}{14x^2} \\[0.8em]
\text{Step 3: } & \text{Combine numerators:} \\
&= \mathbf{\frac{6 + 5x}{14x^2}}
\end{aligned}$$
pitfall: **Power Choice:** In the LCD, choose $x^2$, NOT $x^3$ or $x$! The LCD takes the HIGHEST power present: $14x^2$.
script:
[Prof. Park] Slide 2 presents Section 1.5 Example 3A on workbook page 17: Add and simplify: 3 / (7x^2) + 5 / (14x). Let's find our Least Common Denominator systematically: Look at the numerical coefficients: 7 and 14. 14 is a multiple of 7, so our numerical LCD is 14.

[TA Sora] Look at the variable powers: x^2 and x^1. The highest power is x^2. Combine them: our LCD is 14x^2! Now let's check what each fraction needs: The first fraction is 3 / (7x^2). Its denominator already has x^2, but needs its coefficient scaled from 7 to 14.

[Prof. Park] So we multiply top and bottom by 2/2: (3 Â· 2) / (7x^2 Â· 2) = 6 / (14x^2). The second fraction is 5 / (14x). Its coefficient is already 14, but it only has x to the first power. It needs one more x to reach x^2!

[TA Sora] So we multiply top and bottom by x/x: (5 Â· x) / (14x Â· x) = 5x / (14x^2). Now both fractions share the identical denominator 14x^2.

[Prof. Park] Combine the numerators: 6/(14x^2) + 5x/(14x^2) = (6 + 5x) / (14x^2), which we write in standard order as (5x + 6) / (14x^2). Can we cancel x in 5x with x^2 on the bottom? Never! 5x is part of the sum (5x + 6).

[TA Sora] Unless the entire binomial has a common factor with the denominator, no canceling is allowed. (5x + 6) / (14x^2) is our final answer!

[Prof. Park] Here is my personal study tip for workbook page 17: whenever you see a problem like (A + B)/C - (D + E)/C, draw bright red parentheses around (D + E) before you write another stroke of your pencil!

[TA Sora] That single second of drawing protective parentheses eliminates 90% of all student errors on rational expression exams. Notice also why factoring out the greatest common factor in the numerator is essential: in (4x - 4)/(4x), 4 is a common factor of BOTH terms upstairs. Factoring gives 4(x - 1).

[Prof. Park] That allows the 4 to cancel with the 4 downstairs. If a student simply crosses out the 4x in the front, they leave -4 behind with no denominator, which is an algebraic catastrophe! Always factor before you cancel! No factoring, no cancelling! That is our golden motto!

title: Example 3B: Three-Term Rational Expression with 4th Power
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 10 • Section 1.5 Example 3B (Workbook p. 17)
detail: Lecture 10: Rational Expressions (Higher Powers & Binomial Numerators)
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### Add or subtract the expression and simplify (Workbook p. 17)
$$\frac{2}{x} - \frac{9}{10x^4} + \frac{3}{x}$$
solution:
$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Step 1: } & \text{Notice that } \frac{2}{x} \text{ and } \frac{3}{x} \text{ already have the same denominator!} \\
& \left(\frac{2}{x} + \frac{3}{x}\right) - \frac{9}{10x^4} = \frac{5}{x} - \frac{9}{10x^4} \\[0.8em]
\text{Step 2: } & \text{Find LCD of } x \text{ and } 10x^4: \quad \mathbf{\text{LCD} = 10x^4} \\[0.8em]
\text{Step 3: } & \text{Convert to common denominator:} \\
& \frac{5 \cdot 10x^3}{x \cdot 10x^3} - \frac{9}{10x^4} = \frac{50x^3}{10x^4} - \frac{9}{10x^4} = \mathbf{\frac{50x^3 - 9}{10x^4}}
\end{aligned}$$
pitfall: **Sora's Shortcut:** Always combine like fractions first! Adding $\frac{2}{x} + \frac{3}{x} = \frac{5}{x}$ immediately turns a 3-fraction problem into a simple 2-fraction problem!
script:
[Prof. Park] Let's elevate the challenge with Example 3B on slide 3: a three-term rational expression with a 4th power: Simplify: 2/x - 9 / (10x^4) + 3 / (5x^2). Three fractions at once! Don't let the length intimidate youâour LCD strategy works identically regardless of how many fractions there are.

[TA Sora] Look at the denominators: x, 10x^4, and 5x^2. Step 1: Numerical coefficients are 1, 10, and 5. Multiples of 10 and 5 give a numerical LCD of 10! Step 2: Variable powers are x^1, x^4, and x^2. The highest exponent present is 4! So our variable LCD is x^4.

[Prof. Park] Combining them gives our overall Least Common Denominator: 10x^4! Now let's scale each of the three fractions into equivalent fractions with denominator 10x^4: Fraction 1: 2/x. To turn x into 10x^4, multiply by 10x^3: (2 Â· 10x^3) / (x Â· 10x^3) = 20x^3 / (10x^4). Fraction 2: 9 / (10x^4).

[TA Sora] Its denominator is already 10x^4! It needs no scaling at all. Fraction 3: 3 / (5x^2). To turn 5x^2 into 10x^4, multiply by 2x^2: (3 Â· 2x^2) / (5x^2 Â· 2x^2) = 6x^2 / (10x^4).

[Prof. Park] Now combine all three numerators over the common denominator 10x^4, paying close attention to the operations: The first operation is subtraction, and the second is addition: (20x^3 - 9 + 6x^2) / (10x^4). Rearrange the numerator terms in descending degree order: (20x^3 + 6x^2 - 9) / (10x^4).

[TA Sora] None of the numerator terms can be combined because their degrees are 3, 2, and 0. And 20, 6, and -9 share no common factor with 10. Our three-term rational expression is fully simplified! Look closely at how we simplified (3x + 6) / (3x^2) on slide 3:

[Prof. Park] Notice that we factored out 3 from BOTH terms in the numerator: 3(x + 2). Because 3 is multiplied by (x + 2), 3 is a FACTOR! And 3 in the denominator is also a FACTOR!

[TA Sora] Nowâand ONLY nowâcan the 3 cancel top and bottom, leaving (x + 2) / (x^2)! Factoring first is the only legal ticket to cancelling in rational expressions!

title: Example 3C & 3D: Multi-Term Common Denominators
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 10 • Section 1.5 Example 3C & 3D (Workbook p. 17)
detail: Lecture 10: Rational Expressions (Higher Powers & Binomial Numerators)
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### Add or subtract the expressions (Workbook p. 17)
$$\text{C. } \frac{2}{3b} + \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{6b}$$
$$\text{D. } \frac{2}{5r} - \frac{3}{4r} - \frac{7}{10}$$
solution:
$$\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{Part\ C:}\quad & \text{Combine } b\text{-terms first: } \frac{2}{3b} + \frac{1}{6b} = \frac{4}{6b} + \frac{1}{6b} = \frac{5}{6b} \\
& \text{Now add } \frac{5}{6b} + \frac{1}{4}. \quad \text{LCD of } 6b \text{ and } 4 \text{ is } 12b. \\
&= \frac{5 \cdot 2}{6b \cdot 2} + \frac{1 \cdot 3b}{4 \cdot 3b} = \mathbf{\frac{10 + 3b}{12b}} \\[1em]
\mathbf{Part\ D:}\quad & \text{Combine } r\text{-terms first: } \frac{2}{5r} - \frac{3}{4r} = \frac{8}{20r} - \frac{15}{20r} = \frac{-7}{20r} \\
& \text{Now subtract } \frac{-7}{20r} - \frac{7}{10}. \quad \text{LCD of } 20r \text{ and } 10 \text{ is } 20r. \\
&= \frac{-7}{20r} - \frac{7 \cdot 2r}{10 \cdot 2r} = \mathbf{\frac{-7 - 14r}{20r}}
\end{aligned}$$
pitfall: **Sign Caution:** In Part D, $8 - 15 = -7$. Keep that negative sign in front of the 7!
script:
[Prof. Park] Moving to slide 4, let's examine Examples 3C and 3D: Multi-Term Common Denominators: Part C: 2 / (3b) + 1/4 + 1 / (6b). Sora, walk us through finding the LCD when one term is a pure constant fraction without a variable! That is a wonderful detail to notice!

[TA Sora] The denominators are 3b, 4, and 6b. First, look at the numbers: 3, 4, and 6. Multiples of 6 are 6, 12, 18... 12 is divisible by 3, 4, and 6! So our numerical LCD is 12.

[Prof. Park] Second, look at the variable: b appears to the first power in two denominators. Even though the middle fraction 1/4 has no b, any fraction in the family that needs b must receive b! So our variable LCD is b. Combining them gives an LCD of 12b!

[TA Sora] Let's scale all three fractions to 12b: Fraction 1: 2 / (3b). Multiply top and bottom by 4/4: (2 Â· 4) / (3b Â· 4) = 8 / (12b). Fraction 2: 1/4. To turn 4 into 12b, we must multiply by 3b!

[Prof. Park] Multiply top and bottom by 3b / 3b: (1 Â· 3b) / (4 Â· 3b) = 3b / (12b). Fraction 3: 1 / (6b). Multiply top and bottom by 2/2: (1 Â· 2) / (6b Â· 2) = 2 / (12b).

[TA Sora] Now combine the numerators over 12b: 8 + 3b + 2 = (3b + 10) / (12b). Can we reduce 3b + 10 over 12b? Look at 3, 10, and 12: 3 and 12 share 3, but 10 is not divisible by 3.

[Prof. Park] 10 and 12 share 2, but 3 is not divisible by 2. There is NO common factor shared by all terms. Therefore, (3b + 10) / (12b) is in lowest terms!

[TA Sora] On slide 4, look at the distribution of scaling factors: when multiplying (x + 3) by 3, you must distribute 3 to BOTH x and 3: 3x + 9! And when multiplying (2x - 1) by 2, you must distribute 2 to BOTH 2x and -1: 4x - 2!

[Prof. Park] Never leave a term behind when building equivalent fractions upstairs! In Example 3C, notice the factored form of the final answer: 7(x + 1) / (12x). On exams, both 7(x + 1)/(12x) and (7x + 7)/(12x) are 100% acceptable.

[TA Sora] Factoring out the 7 lets you quickly check whether anything can cancel with the denominator 12x. Since 7 shares no common factor with 12, and (x + 1) does not cancel with x, you know the fraction is irreducible!

[Prof. Park] That is why factoring your final answer gives you an instant built-in correctness check!

title: Example 3E: Subtracting Fractions with Binomial Numerators
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 10 • Section 1.5 Example 3E (Workbook p. 17)
detail: Lecture 10: Rational Expressions (Higher Powers & Binomial Numerators)
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
solution:
$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Step 1: } & \text{Find LCD of } 3x \text{ and } 6x: \quad \mathbf{\text{LCD} = 6x} \\[0.8em]
\text{Step 2: } & \text{Scale the first fraction by } \frac{2}{2}: \\
& \frac{2(2x - 5)}{6x} - \frac{5x + 9}{6x} = \frac{4x - 10}{6x} - \frac{5x + 9}{6x} \\[0.8em]
\text{Step 3: } & \text{Combine with parentheses to distribute the minus sign!} \\
&= \frac{(4x - 10) - (5x + 9)}{6x} \\
&= \frac{4x - 10 - 5x - 9}{6x} = \mathbf{\frac{-x - 19}{6x}}
\end{aligned}$$
pitfall: **EXAM DISASTER ALERT:** Writing $4x - 10 - 5x + 9$. The minus MUST hit both $5x$ and $+9$, turning $+9$ into $-9$! So $-10 - 9 = -19$!
script:
[Prof. Park] Now we arrive at slide 5, which features the single most critical problem type in Section 1.5: Example 3E: Subtracting Fractions with Binomial Numerators: (2x - 5) / (3x) - (5x + 9) / (6x). Sound the emergency siren!

[TA Sora] This is where hundreds of algebra students lose points on Exam 1! Why? Because of that minus sign between the fractions! When you subtract a fraction whose numerator is a binomial, that minus sign MUST distribute to EVERY term in the numerator!

[Prof. Park] Sora's Golden Rule: Immediately wrap every binomial numerator in protective parentheses before you do anything else: [ (2x - 5) ] / (3x) - [ (5x + 9) ] / (6x)! Let's find the LCD first. The denominators are 3x and 6x.

[TA Sora] 6 is a multiple of 3, and both have x to the first power. So our Least Common Denominator is 6x! The second fraction already has 6x.

[Prof. Park] For the first fraction, we must multiply top and bottom by 2/2: 2 Â· (2x - 5) / (3x Â· 2) = (4x - 10) / (6x). Now place both numerators over the common denominator 6x: [ (4x - 10) - (5x + 9) ] / (6x).

[TA Sora] Look at that second set of parentheses: - (5x + 9). Distribute the minus sign: -5x - 9! So our numerator becomes: 4x - 10 - 5x - 9. Now combine like terms: 4x - 5x = -x. And -10 - 9 = -19!

[Prof. Park] So our numerator is -x - 19. Over the common denominator 6x, our final answer is: (-x - 19) / (6x) (or - (x + 19) / (6x)). If a student failed to distribute the negative, they would get -10 + 9 = -1, which is completely wrong.

[TA Sora] Protective parentheses save the day! Let us review the test value check on slide 5: why is plugging in x = 1 such an incredible strategy? On an exam, you don't have an answer key in the back of the book.

[Prof. Park] But by spending 30 seconds plugging in x = 1 into both the original problem and your simplified answer, if the two values match, you know with 100% mathematical certainty that your answer is correct! It gives you total peace of mind before turning in your exam paper.

[TA Sora] Remember that the negative sign applies to the ENTIRE quantity (5x + 9), so both signs flip: -5x - 9! That gives -10 - 9 = -19. If you got -1, you forgot to distribute the negative sign! Always double-check every sign distribution!

title: Example 3F: Second Binomial Subtraction Master Problem
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 10 • Section 1.5 Example 3F (Workbook p. 17)
detail: Lecture 10: Rational Expressions (Higher Powers & Binomial Numerators)
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
solution:
$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Step 1: } & \text{Find LCD of } 8y \text{ and } 4y: \quad \mathbf{\text{LCD} = 8y} \\[0.8em]
\text{Step 2: } & \text{Scale the second fraction by } \frac{2}{2}: \\
& \frac{3y + 7}{8y} - \frac{2(9y - 11)}{8y} = \frac{3y + 7}{8y} - \frac{18y - 22}{8y} \\[0.8em]
\text{Step 3: } & \text{Combine and distribute the subtraction:} \\
&= \frac{(3y + 7) - (18y - 22)}{8y} \\
&= \frac{3y + 7 - 18y + 22}{8y} \\
&= \mathbf{\frac{-15y + 29}{8y}}
\end{aligned}$$
pitfall: **Double Negative Alert:** $-(-22) = +22$! So $7 + 22 = +29$! Do not write $7 - 22 = -15$!
script:
[Prof. Park] To conclude Lecture 10, let's look at slide 6: Example 3F on workbook page 17âour Second Binomial Subtraction Master Problem: (3y + 7) / (8y) - (9y - 11) / (4y).

[TA Sora] Let's apply our bulletproof procedure: Step 1: Wrap the binomial numerators in protective parentheses: [ (3y + 7) ] / (8y) - [ (9y - 11) ] / (4y). Step 2: Find the LCD. The denominators are 8y and 4y.

[Prof. Park] 8 is a multiple of 4, so our LCD is 8y! Step 3: Scale the second fraction. To turn 4y into 8y, multiply top and bottom by 2/2: 2 Â· (9y - 11) / (4y Â· 2) = (18y - 22) / (8y).

[TA Sora] Now write over the single common denominator 8y: [ (3y + 7) - (18y - 22) ] / (8y). Distribute the negative sign to the second numerator: - (18y - 22) becomes -18y + 22! Notice that -(-22) became POSITIVE 22!

[Prof. Park] That double negative turning into +22 is where the magic happens! Now combine like terms in the numerator: 3y - 18y = -15y. +7 + 22 = +29! So our numerator is -15y + 29 (or 29 - 15y).

[TA Sora] Over the common denominator 8y, our final simplified answer is: (-15y + 29) / (8y)! Can we cancel the y in 15y with the y in 8y? No! -15y is tied to 29 by addition. No canceling is possible.

[Prof. Park] That brings us to the conclusion of Lecture 10 and the complete mastery of Section 1.5! In Lecture 11, we will begin Section 1.6 on workbook page 18: Solving Linear Equations. Outstanding job everyone, and we will see you in Lecture 11!

[TA Sora] Let us review the full 4-step checklist for adding and subtracting rational expressions:
1. Wrap all binomial numerators in protective parentheses! 2. Find the LCD of all denominators (LCM of numbers, highest power of variables). 3. Scale each fraction top and bottom by its missing factors. 4.

[Prof. Park] Distribute and combine like terms over the single LCD, and factor to check for final simplification! With that checklist, you are fully equipped for any rational expression problem. We look forward to seeing you in Lecture 11 for linear equations!
